title: Six ways to be dear
hook: kindness in deed, word and thought, sharing, virtue and view held together

segments.voice: Yesterday: the nuns, the scattered mind, and your line, inspired, then calm. What lifted you? Today, from one mind to a whole community, and what keeps people close. Day six hundred seventy-five.

Every group that lasts, a family, a team, a congregation, a group chat that's somehow survived ten years, has some unspoken reasons it holds together. And every group that falls apart has reasons too. The early monastic community knew both. Monks quarreled; the texts don't hide it. So in the Book of Sixes, the Buddha names six qualities that, in his words, are worth remembering, because they create love and respect and lead to harmony, to unity, to not quarreling. The Pali name is saraniya: things to be remembered, or things that make you dear. Today: six ways to be dear.
screen: `WHY GROUPS HOLD TOGETHER.` → `MONKS QUARRELED TOO.` → `SIX THINGS TO REMEMBER.`

segments.voice: The first three are about kindness, in three directions. One: acts of body done with loving-kindness toward your companions, both in public and in private. Two: words spoken with loving-kindness, both in public and in private. Three: thoughts held with loving-kindness, both in public and in private. That little phrase, in public and in private, is the heart of it. Anyone can be kind when watched. What builds trust is the kindness nobody sees. Four: sharing. Whatever you receive, even the contents of your alms bowl, you share it with those who keep the same practice, without holding back. Imagine a monk with one bowl of food a day, splitting it. Five: virtue held in common. You keep the same precepts as your companions, unbroken, the kind the wise praise. Six: view held in common. You share the understanding that leads out of suffering. Notice how practical the order is. It starts with what everyone can do immediately, a kind act, a kind word, and moves toward what takes years, a shared way of seeing. And notice that none of the six is about getting others to like you. They're all things you give. Being dear, in this sutta, isn't something you chase. It's what grows around someone who acts, speaks and thinks with kindness, shares, and keeps faith with a common path.
screen: `KIND IN DEED, WORD, THOUGHT.` · `IN PUBLIC AND IN PRIVATE.` · `SHARE EVEN YOUR BOWL.` · then, large: `VIRTUE AND VIEW IN COMMON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: share one thing. Sit, and settle. Bring to mind a group you belong to: a family, a workplace, a team, a circle of friends. Picture the faces. Now think of one thing you have that you could share with them today. Some food. Some time. A tool, a skill, a piece of good news, credit for a job well done. Picture offering it, freely, without keeping score. Then, for a breath or two, wish them all well, quietly, in private. The bell holds the time.
Six ways to be dear. Kindness in body, speech and mind, public and private; sharing; virtue in common; view in common: the six things that create love and harmony. Today's word.
screen: `SIX WAYS TO BE DEAR — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: six ways to be dear. Today, do one kind thing for someone in your group that nobody will see. Day six hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: Buddhist monastic communities often teach the six saraniya dhammas as the basis of harmony in the sangha, and lay Buddhist groups sometimes take them as guidelines for family and community life.

fork.setup: you're a monk with one bowl of food for the day. a companion who keeps the same practice has nothing. what does the sutta describe?
options: keep it; you need your strength.
fork.reveal: the fourth way to be dear is sharing whatever you receive, even the contents of your bowl, freely with your companions.

original.note: Pali saraniya: to be remembered, cordial; the saraniya dhamma are qualities that make people dear to each other.

trapdoor: what you thought: a community holds together through rules.
what it means: AN 6.12 names six things that make people dear: kindness, sharing, virtue and view in common.
what a scholar hears: the same six appear in the Digha Nikaya's account of the Buddha's last days, among the conditions for the community's welfare.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 16 (Mahaparinibbana Sutta), conditions of welfare

notes: AN 6.12 paraphrased. Confirm numbering (AN 6.11 and 6.12 both carry the saraniya list in some editions).
Confirm that DN 16 includes the six saraniya dhammas among the conditions of welfare (trapdoor).
Confirm Devanagari सारणीय and the gloss 'to be remembered / making dear'.
